title: Cheapest Walk Down and Right
statement:
You get a grid grid of non-negative integers. Each number is the toll for stepping on that cell.

You start on the top-left cell and must reach the bottom-right cell. On every move you go one cell right or one cell down; nothing else is allowed.

The cost of a walk is the sum of the tolls of every cell it touches, including the first and the last cell. Return the cheapest possible cost.

examples.why: Always taking the cheaper next cell goes 1 → 1 → 8 → 1 → 1 = 12. Paying 6 early to go down the left edge costs 1 + 6 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 10.
With one row there is only one walk, and it touches every cell.

hints: The last move into any cell came either from the cell above or the cell to the left.
If you knew the cheapest cost to reach the cell above and the cell to the left, what is the cheapest cost to reach this one?
Fill a table row by row: best[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(best[r−1][c], best[r][c−1]), treating cells outside the grid as unreachable. One row of the table is enough.

explain.intuition:
Picking the cheaper neighbour at each step fails, as the second example shows: a toll you avoid now can trap you in an expensive corridor later. Instead, ask the question backwards. Any walk into cell (r, c) arrives from above or from the left. So the cheapest way to reach (r, c) is its own toll plus the cheaper of the cheapest ways to reach those two cells.

Filling cells in reading order guarantees both of those answers already exist when you need them. Each cell is computed once, and you only ever look at the previous row, so a single array of length cols is enough.
steps: First row: each cell can only be reached from the left, so best[c] = best[c − 1] + grid[0][c] (and best[0] = grid[0][0]).

For each later row: best[0] += grid[r][0] (only from above), then for c ≥ 1, best[c] = grid[r][c] + min(best[c], best[c − 1]). Here best[c] still holds the row above and best[c − 1] already holds this row.
pitfalls: Greedily stepping to the cheaper neighbour. It ignores what lies beyond that neighbour.
Forgetting the edges: cells in the first row or first column have only one way in. Treating the missing neighbour as cost 0 lets the walk come from outside the grid.
Leaving out the toll of the starting cell or the final cell.

solutions.title: Try every walk
solutions.idea: Recursively try going right and going down from every cell and keep the cheaper total. Exponential, but it states the rule directly.

solutions.title: Full table
solutions.idea: best[r][c] is the cheapest cost to reach (r, c). It equals the toll plus the cheaper of the cell above and the cell to the left.

solutions.title: One row of the table
solutions.idea: Only the previous row is ever read, so overwrite a single array in place, left to right.

followups: Also return the walk itself as a list of moves. What do you need to remember per cell?
Some cells are walls you cannot enter. How does the recurrence change, and what do you return if the goal is unreachable?
Moves in all four directions are now allowed. Why does this table stop working, and what replaces it? (Hint: Dijkstra.)
